extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of satire; scholars and students of Rabelais and bawdy Renaissance comic prose
extracted.subtask_description: Producing satirical, bawdy, grotesque comic prose in the Renaissance/early-modern tradition — using obscene bodily detail, practical jokes, learned parody, tall-tale exaggeration, and episodic anecdotes to generate humor and social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire of institutions and clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mocking and exposing the hypocrisy, gullibility, and corruption of religious and civic institutions (pardoners, friars, courts, university sophisters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ridicule of pardoners and relics (taking money at boxes), the friar stripped by sewn vestments revealing his genitals in church, legal suits to force fashion changes, and sly explanations that re-interpret Latin phrases to justify theft (Centuplum accipies → Centuplum accipe). Use concrete comic incidents that reveal institutional folly and hypocrisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bawdy and obscene bodily humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of explicit sexual and scatological imagery (genital references, pox, postern blasts, farting) as a primary source of comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: continuous references to privy parts of women, flies attracted to wounds, ‘he would fart like a horse’, and graphic descriptions of pox and boils. Deploy shocking, earthy detail to produce laughter and transgressive satire; normalize vulgar terms within narratorial voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolic exaggeration / tall tale
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate overstatement and fantastical scaling (walls made of women's privates, wounds that hold cartloads of moss, claims of fantastic wealth) to create absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: building fortifications from 'sine quo nons' of women; lion's wound holding 'above two cartloads of moss'; Panurge's boastful tall tales about pensions and sums. Exaggeration should be sustained and grounded in ludicrous specifics to maximize comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-joke repertoire (trickster antics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy built from a catalogue of sneaky pranks and contraptions: itching powders, greasing clothes, picklocks, squibs, fleas, hooked buckles, burning glasses, and staged physical traps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panurge's pockets of tricks and his routines (greasing gowns, casting itching powder, fixing carts to overthrow watchmen, cutting stirrup-leathers) illustrate how an inventor of pranks functions as a comedic engine. Use an inventory of devices and set-pieces; show consequences and social disruption for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cataloguing / list humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Long, cumulative lists of items, maladies, tricks, numbers, or attributes used to produce comic accumulation and rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: inventories of Panurge's pockets and their contents; counts like 'three score and three tricks', lists of victims and maladies. Use piling, increasingly absurd entries, and numerical specificity to amplify comedic momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-learned language and classical parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodying erudition by mixing actual scholarly references, Latinisms, and invented pseudo-scholarly terms to comic effect and to satirize pretension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: citations of Beda, Proclus, Artemidorus, and uses of words like 'sine quo nons, kallibistris, or contrapunctums'; Panurge and others use learned registers to justify base actions. Juxtapose high-learned diction with vulgar action or twist scholarly claims into absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropomorphism / fable devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Using talking animals and fable-like episodes (lion, fox, etc.) to stage allegory, moral inversion, and comic exempla.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'In the time that the beasts did speak' — the lion, fox, and carpenter enact a grotesque, instructive anecdote about wounds and wiping. Employ animals behaving as humans to distance and highlight satirical points while keeping the tone comic and proverbial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization through grotesque detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Building comic characters by enumerating bodily, moral, and behavioral peculiarities in vivid, often disgusting or indecorous detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panurge is defined by his middle stature, aquiline nose, lechery, and an exhaustive list of petty, filthy practices and accoutrements. Use rich, concrete, often repulsive specifics to make a character memorably comic and to justify their antics.

rubrics_metrics.name: High/low juxtaposition (comic dissonance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasting lofty philosophical or scholarly conversation with base, vulgar, or bodily action to produce irony and ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Thaumast cites Plato and arguments by signs while Panurge and Pantagruel engage in farting, pranks, and crude talk. Place grand rhetoric or learned debate next to coarse behavior to undercut seriousness and elicit laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and imperative rhythm for comic timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of repeated commands, catchphrases, and reiterated verbs to create rhythm and escalating comic insistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the lion repeatedly urging 'Wipe, my friend, wipe' builds a comic ritual and growing discomfort; Panurge's repeated exhortations to prank or mock create timing. Repetition can emphasize absurdity and create comic cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque imagery employed as social commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurd, grotesque proposals or images serve as satirical critiques of social practices, military logic, fashions, or customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proposing walls built from women's privy parts satirizes civic defense and social values; other grotesqueries expose social hypocrisy. Use grotesque metaphor and parody policy/logic to reveal underlying follies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick and physical-comedy set-pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Fast, violent, or pratfall incidents (overturning carts, cutting stirrups, explosive squibs) used for immediate, visual comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tumbril/dung-cart hurled to overthrow watchmen, cutting the stirrup-leather so a councillor falls. Stage clear physical cause-and-effect mishaps, minimal subtlety, and visible consequences to produce broad laughter.
